analysis.one_liner: Adds a small tax on stock, bond, and derivative trades to fund public investment.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee assignment and received no vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would place a small fee on each trade of stocks, bonds, derivatives, and certain digital assets — 0.5% of a stock's value, 0.10% on bonds, and 0.005% on derivatives [S3]. The tax is collected by exchanges and brokers at the moment of the trade [S3]. It would exempt initial stock offerings, very short-term debt, and routine securities lending, and it would refund the tax to individual investors earning under $50,000 ($75,000 for couples) [S2] [S3]. Revenue would go to the general fund for public investment; the bill's stated purpose includes investing in families, infrastructure, and reducing market volatility [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, if the revenue is spent on public priorities the bill names — families, infrastructure, environment, and financial security [S3]. Small individual investors are directly shielded: anyone earning under the income limits gets the tax they paid refunded through a tax credit [S3]. The tax is aimed at high-volume trading, where the largest cost falls on firms that trade millions of times a day.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 0.5% excise tax on stock trades, 0.10% on bond transfers, and 0.005% on derivatives, generating federal revenue each time a security changes hands [S3].
Refunds the tax through a credit to individuals with modified adjusted gross income under $50,000 ($75,000 joint), so small retirement and personal accounts are not the ones paying it [S2] [S3].

Excludes initial stock and bond issuances, short-term debt maturing in 60 days or less, and standard securities lending, so the tax targets secondary-market trading rather than companies raising capital [S2] [S3].
States its purpose as raising money to invest in families, communities, infrastructure, and the environment, and to reduce market volatility [S3].

analysis.who_pays: High-volume traders, hedge funds, proprietary trading desks at large banks, and other large institutional investors bear the cost, since the tax applies to every covered purchase whether by a U.S. facility or a U.S. person [S3]. Index funds, mutual funds, and pension funds trading on behalf of savers would pay the tax on each trade, a cost that can flow back to account holders. Ordinary people trading their own accounts are refunded through the credit [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax applies to every purchase of covered securities, including by mutual funds, index funds, and pension funds trading for millions of savers, so a share of the cost can be passed to retirement and 401(k) accounts even though individual direct investors get a refund credit [S3].

Because the tax applies only to trades cleared on U.S. facilities or involving a U.S. person, trading could shift to foreign venues; the bill directs the Treasury Secretary to write regulations to prevent avoidance, including through non-U.S. persons, but leaves the design to future rulemaking [S3].
The tax raises the cost of all portfolio rebalancing, including for bond traders; bonds are taxed at a lower 0.10% rate but there is no credit for larger savers above the income limits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is deliberately protective of ordinary investors: initial offerings are exempt so companies raising capital are untouched, and small savers are made whole by the credit [S3]. The main real cost is on institutional portfolios held for savers, and the main design risk is enforcement against offshore avoidance, which depends on regulations not yet written [S3]. The tradeoff is a small per-trade cost on the financial industry in exchange for federal revenue, and the record does not include a revenue estimate to weigh precisely.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2023, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended in January 2025 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill on June 14, 2023, with Padilla as cosponsor [S1] [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
The Finance Committee held no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill, and the full Senate never considered it; the Congress ended January 3, 2025 without any further action [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The financial trading industry — high-frequency trading firms, hedge funds, and large institutional desks — is better off because the bill never moved, since it would have paid the tax on every covered trade. Ordinary taxpayers are no better off, as no revenue was raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High-volume trading firms and hedge funds

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Tax on Wall Street Speculation Act on June 14, 2023.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no markup, hearing, or vote — after it was referred on June 14, 2023.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the only recorded support came from a progressive independent and one Democrat, so the partisan shape of a floor fight was never tested.

industries.note: A 0.5% tax on every stock purchase hits firms that trade thousands of times a day hardest, and the bill was explicitly framed as a tax on speculation [S3]. The tax's cost falls almost entirely on this industry, which is why it is the clearest beneficiary of the bill's death.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and large asset managers
industries.note: Every portfolio trade becomes taxable, raising the cost of running large funds. Fund investors above the income limits receive no credit, so some cost passes to savers through fund fees or returns.

The bill makes exchanges and brokers the collection point for the tax, adding a compliance duty [S3]. They keep their trading business but absorb reporting and remittance work, and could lose some volume to offshore venues the bill's anti-avoidance rules try to reach.
Initial issuances of stock, partnership interests, and digital assets are exempt, so companies going public or issuing new shares pay nothing [S3].
